title: A Lone Solution
statement:
Let $i = \sqrt{-1}$. For an integer $k$, consider the following system in the complex number $z$:

$$\begin{aligned}
|z - 3 + 8i| &= 20, \\
|z - k| + |z - k - 6 - 8i| &= 10.
\end{aligned}$$

Find the number of integers $k$ for which this system has exactly one solution $z$.
hints: Look at the two fixed points in the second equation, $k$ and $k + 6 + 8i$. How far apart are they, and how does that distance compare with the $10$ on the right-hand side?

The points $k$ and $k + 6 + 8i$ are exactly $10$ apart, so the equality case of the triangle inequality shows that the second equation describes a line segment rather than an ellipse. Write this segment as $z = k + s(6 + 8i)$ with $0 \le s \le 1$, then substitute it into the circle equation.

Substituting $z = k + s(6 + 8i)$ gives $f(s) = 100s^2 + (12k + 92)s + (k - 3)^2 - 336 = 0$, and we need the number of roots with $0 \le s \le 1$. Here $f(0) = (k - 3)^2 - 336$, $f(1) = (k + 3)^2 - 144$, and the discriminant is $256(34 - k)(k + 16)$. Use the signs of these three quantities to sort the integers $k$ into cases. Then count the values of $k$ that give exactly one root in the interval.
solution: Let $A = k$ and $B = k + 6 + 8i$, so that $|A - B| = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = 10$. By the triangle inequality, $|z - A| + |z - B| \ge |A - B| = 10$, with equality exactly when $z$ lies on the closed segment $AB$. So the second equation says that $z = k + s(6 + 8i)$ for some $0 \le s \le 1$, and different values of $s$ give different points $z$. The first equation describes the circle with centre $3 - 8i$ and radius $20$. Substituting the segment into it gives $(k - 3 + 6s)^2 + (8 + 8s)^2 = 400$, which is $f(s) = 0$, where $$f(s) = 100s^2 + (12k + 92)s + (k - 3)^2 - 336.$$ We must therefore count the integers $k$ for which $f$ has exactly one root in $[0, 1]$. We have $f(0) = (k - 3)^2 - 336$ and $f(1) = (k + 3)^2 - 144$, and the discriminant of $f$ is $$(12k + 92)^2 - 400\left((k - 3)^2 - 336\right) = 256(34 - k)(k + 16).$$ Since $18^2 < 336 < 19^2$, we have $f(0) < 0$ exactly when $-15 \le k \le 21$. Also, $f(1) < 0$ exactly when $-14 \le k \le 8$, and $f(1) = 0$ exactly when $k = -15$ or $k = 9$. Because $f$ is a quadratic with positive leading coefficient, $f(0) < 0$ implies that it has exactly one positive root. Every integer $k$ falls into one of the following cases. Case $-14 \le k \le 8$. Here $f(0) < 0$ and $f(1) < 0$. Since $f$ is convex, $f < 0$ on all of $[0, 1]$, so there is no solution. Case $k = -15$ or $k = 9$. Here $f(0) < 0$ and $f(1) = 0$. The unique positive root is $s = 1$, so there is exactly one solution. This gives $2$ values of $k$. Case $10 \le k \le 21$. Here $f(0) < 0$ and $f(1) > 0$. The unique positive root lies in $(0, 1)$, so there is exactly one solution. This gives $12$ values of $k$. Case $k \ge 22$. All three coefficients of $f$ are positive, because $(k - 3)^2 \ge 361 > 336$ and $12k + 92 > 0$. Hence $f(s) > 0$ for all $s \ge 0$, so there is no solution. Case $k = -16$. The discriminant is $0$, so $f$ has a double root at $s = \frac{100}{200} = \frac{1}{2}$. This lies in $[0, 1]$, so the segment touches the circle at its midpoint and there is exactly one solution. This gives $1$ value of $k$. Case $k \le -17$. Here $34 - k > 0$ and $k + 16 < 0$, so the discriminant is negative and $f$ has no real roots. There is no solution. The total number of integers $k$ is $2 + 12 + 1$, so the answer is $15$. Why this works. triangle-inequality, quadratic-discriminant: the equality case turns the apparent ellipse into a segment, and the discriminant detects the one tangency that the endpoint signs cannot see.
